SPOILER ALERT: The story includes details about Season 5 of Netflix‘s Outer Banks.
There were a lot of full-circle elements in the fifth and final season of Outer Banks.
The series ended the way it started, with a hurricane. Sarah (Madelyn Cline) wore a version of her iconic Midsummers white dress from Season 1 to her wedding to John B (Chase Stokes) in the series finale where the two recited the vows she used for their impromptu nuptials on the open seas in Season 2. And the Pogues, in the same lineup as their very first treasure hunt (sans the late JJ), went on one final adventure together in Azerbaijan.
It wasn’t your typical Outer Banks season: there were three proposals — two by Pope (Jonathan Daviss) to Cleo (Carlacia Grant), one by Rafe (Drew Starkey) to Sofia (Fiona Palomo), a wedding (Sarah and John B) and a baby, as the couple welcomed a son whom, as expected, they named JJ, after their beloved friend who was supposed to be the baby’s godfather.
Watch on Deadline
The show leaned into the supernatural, too, with Kiara, JJ’s father Chandler Groff (J. Anthony Crane) and rich collector Finch all chasing Blackbeard’s Blue Crown to try and resurrect a loved one: JJ; Groff’s wife (and JJ’s mother), whom he had killed; and Finch’s young daughter, respectively. (Groff also senselessly killed JJ, but he didn’t seem to feel remorse over that.)
Holding the crown, Kiara did see JJ under a meteor shower, but it was her memories of him. The season also had a revenge thriller vibe as, in her grief, Kiara went full Kill Bill on Groff, chasing him down to murder him, which she did on her second try.
Ultimately, it was a happy ending for the Pogues who were able to get back one of the many treasures they had discovered only to see them being taken away – the Royal Merchant gold — which they recovered from the bottom of the ocean after the boat Groff and Kiara were on sunk in the hurricane. Kiara managed to stay afloat while waiting for the Pogues to rescue her as she found herself in calm waters under the eye of the storm. This was the second time she cheated death, having been sent to the bottom of the ocean by Groff in an earlier episode, summoning JJ for help both times.
With the money from the gold, the Pogues “rebuilt the island the way it should be so all of us, Kooks and Pogues, could live there… forever,” as John B said at the end of the finale. On the new Kildare, Kooks largely bailed out, Pogues moved in, Pope and Cleo settled into his ancestral home, Tannyhill, and Topper is a bartender.
In an interview with Deadline, Outer Banks creators Josh Pate, Jonas Pate and Shannon Burke discuss the ending, what parts of it they had conceived years ago and what elements they had added more recently. They also answer burning questions about the fate of some characters, including what happened to Rafe and Sofia, and whether Sarah and Rafe’s stepmother Rose got any of the gold she had kept until Groff stole it from her.
Each Outer Banks character had their own ending, many of which converged at John B and Sarah’s wedding.
The trio also explain whether they ever considered bringing JJ back from the dead or have Rudy Pankow reprise his role in any way, if they thought of killing off another Pogue and why Groff was so unredeemable.
As part of the interview, Josh and Jonas Pate and Burke also revealed that a prequel set 20 years prior, which features the Outer Banks parents’ generation, is in active development at Netflix.
“It really is the story of how the island split — and it’s particularly relevant in our country right now — how it split into the haves and have-nots, how the Kooks and the Pogues started,” Josh Pate said. “How did this rift start?”
Below, they tease another possible spinoff.
Ending On a Win
DEADLINE: Let’s start with with the ending. You said after Season 4 that you’re “bringing it all home.” Is this what you envision, building a Kildare utopia with Kooks and Pogues living in harmony?
JONAS PATE: Yes.
JOSH PATE: I don’t think the Kooks are there anymore. I think the Kooks have all been kind of driven off.
JONAS PATE: No, no, no. There are some, maybe we have a disagreement on that. But I think it’s the happiest ending you could possibly have. Everybody’s there living together. We had lost for 49 straight episodes, so we feel like we earned the happy ending.
JOSH PATE: I agree. I think it’s a happy ending, and that’s what we wanted it to be — as happy as we could make it, given everything that had happened in the story.
DEADLINE: Is this ending in the ballpark of what you had envisioned from the beginning, from when you created the show?
BURKE: It is. Many elements of the final sequence, we discussed at the end of Season 1.
DEADLINE: Like Sarah and John B’s wedding?
BURKE: Yeah, all that. Tannyhill going to Pope. We sort of knew that it got some traction after Season 1, so we long-arced it from there. So we knew this is where we were going the whole time.
JONAS PATE: And bookending with a hurricane, getting an ending with a hurricane. That was pretty much an original idea because [the series] starts with a hurricane.
DEADLINE: I thought you were going to end it with the Pogues on the beach after the storm and recreate that power outage photo that became the inspiration for the show. Did you think about ending the series with that shot?
JOSH PATE: No, that’s a good question, though. I wish you’d been around. That’s a great idea.
JONAS PATE: Do you want to be on the writers staff for the prequel?
DEADLINE: Was there anything in the ending that changed from the way you had originally planned it?
JOSH PATE: I think Rafe was a big change. I don’t think that at the beginning we had thought that Rafe would be as big a character as he became, as much as we started to really like Drew. Would you guys say that’s fair? I think that evolved.
JONAS PATE: Yeah, and I’d say Pope and Cleo. Both of them had real distinct journeys over this year particularly and I would say that that is more reacting to what happened to Pope in the final episode of the last season and just following it through.
Where In the World Is Rafe?
DEADLINE: Speaking of Rafe, was it deliberate that we never heard from him again? He was supposed to send the gang a postcard from Rio, that didn’t happen. He and Sofia left literally with just the shirts on their backs. Where are they? Are they in South America?
JOSH PATE: That is another spinoff possibility.
JONAS PATE: In the credits, you see a video call from Rafe at the wedding.
DEADLINE: Yes, but we still didn’t get an update. Did he and Sofia get a cut from the gold?
JOSH PATE: Good question. I don’t know. We sort of felt like just Rafe not being arrested for murder, that’s his win. He’s not in jail for the rest of his life.
DEADLINE: Still, it feels sad for him not being able to walk his sister down the aisle.
BURKE: The intent was, it felt like as good as you could possibly get for someone who was so bad for a lot of the series. It was as realistic as you can get with him being as bad as he had been, and so we wanted to thread the needle where he had to pay to some extent. He’s exiled, but he does get a second chance.
Death Does Not Become Pogues
DEADLINE: After JJ’s death in the Season 4 finale, did you consider killing off another Pogue in Season 5? You flirted with Kiara, who came very close to dying twice.
JONAS PATE: Josh, we never thought of killing anybody else, do you remember?
JOSH PATE: I never recall any. I didn’t want to kill anybody, I don’t want anyone else to die.
JONAS PATE: I didn’t think so either. I was just trying to think, like, ‘Did we ever think about it?’ I don’t think so either. Though I would say that something’s thought about at all times. Like, you always consider, everything’s thought of at some point.
OGs-Only Treasure Hunt
DEADLINE: In Season 5, Cleo was sidelined in the Bahamas twice. For the trip to Azerbaijan, Rafe also had a reason to stay, so the Pogues went after the Blue Crown in their original formation (sans JJ). it felt like a throwback to Season 1 and one last adventure for the OGs. Was it intentional?
JOSH PATE: Yeah, I think we’re trying to chime some old vibes, classic OBX vibes on some of this season.
BURKE: And also it gave Cleo a real singular moment where she did something at the end of eight on the runway, and it also set up finishing the Pope and Cleo story. But yeah, it felt good to have just the OG Pogues on one adventure. Jonas, what do you think about that?
JONAS PATE: Yeah, I liked it. I mean, the whole show, honestly, was such a blessing to shoot. The process of making it was so much fun for all of us that I think that we wanted to make sure we experienced all those types of things that we had felt over the course of the season. So it was a little bit of adventure, a little bit of stuff in their home on their home turf. We tried to, as Josh said, chime all the old school, the old versions that we had done in the final season, just to make fans feel satisfied.
Twinkie Lives On
DEADLINE: You mentioned Cleo’s heroics, which included blowing up John B’s beloved VW van Twinkie. It made a return, first in the form of Sarah and John B’s wedding cake, and then as their Just Married van. Was this the refurbished original one or a new incarnation of Twinkie?
JONAS PATE: Nellie, you really watched this, I appreciate that. It was a new incarnation of Twinkie, which is not easy to find. Over the course of the season, I think there were seven, because they kept breaking down. We had to keep replacing them.
Outer Banks or Outer Realm
DEADLINE: Blue Crown’s supposed powers. Why did you decide to introduce the element of immortality and did you consider at any point taking a supernatural route and bringing JJ or somebody else back to life?
JOSH PATE: Actually, there’s a similar supernatural element in earlier seasons with [Carla] Limbrey. We always knew that the show was not a supernatural show but some people believe supernatural things in the world, and these kids could believe in these myths without us actually crossing the line into actual magic, which we never wanted to do.
JONAS PATE: But we felt like, to your point, Josh, it’s human to be superstitious, right? I mean, that’s what a lot of religion is. So we never thought about crossing the line, but we knew that we could have characters that could believe in those types of things, and it could motivate their actions.
BURKE: And we wanted to walk right up to the edge of that line, to the point of where some people believed that it was supernatural, and some people didn’t. We wanted to get right up to the edge of that line, but then not cross it.
DEADLINE: So the ball of light, was it just a natural phenomenon? Because it wasn’t just Kiara; Finch, Groff and others also believed in the crown’s powers.
BURKE: I would say in the staff or the people who are on this phone call that some people here thought it was supernatural, and some people thought it wasn’t. Would you say that’s true, guys? Because I said not supernatural, and I think Jonas said it wasn’t, and Josh, I don’t know what you say.
JOAH PATE: I don’t think it was. I mean, it was a meteor shower. But again, two people can see the same thing, like a lightning bolt, and one can take it in a supernatural, spiritual way, as a sign or a message, and someone else can just be like, “Oh, it’s a lightning bolt.” People can interpret those two things differently.
So, I think there are characters in the show that are on both sides of that fence, and all you have to do is show. It is coincidental? Well, they knew that there was a meteor shower. There was an incredible video that was captured online of this blue light during a meteor shower that basically was the template for the way we did that. That was real, so we didn’t push it that much if you’ve actually seen this one video of this girl underneath a meteor shower.
JJ’s Presence
DEADLINE: So there was no consideration of bringing back JJ at any point, right?
BURKE: Not in any corporeal, like not as a real person, but maybe in a dream sequence, sort of as it was.
DEADLINE: But even in the flashbacks, you had younger actors portraying JJ and Kiara’s early years. Was there a conversation with Rudy to come back?
JOSH PATE: Honestly, not really. We always knew we wanted to show when they first met. I don’t know, maybe glancingly, but it never got very serious.
DEADLINE: In another natural-adjacent phenomenon, Kiara found herself in the eye of a hurricane when she fell overboard, which likely saved her life. It was a beautiful moment but was this supposed to be just symbolic or do we think JJ helped?
BURKE: It’s what you think. Like Josh said, it’s walking right up the line, and you can think one thing or the other. Probably everyone is going to look at that and have a different interpretation. Did he really help or was it just that the eye of a storm passed over?
DEADLINE: Do you have the answer?
JONAS PATE: I guess I know what I think, but that’s not… .
JOSH PATE: I think I know what Kara thinks.
DEADLINE: What does she think?
JOSH PATE: She thinks JJ helped her.
Legalizing the Gold
DEADLINE: I am a little confused how Rose couldn’t legalize the Royal Merchant gold for so long, and our guys did it in no time, becoming very rich.
JOSH PATE: Shan, you want to take that one? Nellie, you’re just grinding us here.
BURNE: We’d have to look that up. In maritime law, if you find it on land, there’s different laws. They were saying that before it was found in someone’s house, they didn’t own that house. The gold goes to the person who is from the house, but now that’s a treasure that they found underwater. That’s a maritime treasure, and I think it goes to them. But I’d have to check that to make sure. It’s a good question. But until proven otherwise, it’s because they found it in water, not on land.
DEADLINE: Well, they didn’t have witnesses, so I don’t think anybody knows where they found it. And the gold was on land before getting on that boat but OK, I’m not going to go down that rabbit hole.
JONAS PATE: In the scene between Rafe and Rose, she says that Ward hadn’t bought the Crain House yet, and they would backdate the sale that so when he found it, that’s his, that it came with the property.
Rose Gold
DEADLINE: Speaking of Rose, the Pogues rightfully scoffed when she asked them to bring her back some gold for a cut. But then we saw her at the wedding, and she kissed John B. So are they on good terms? Did she get any money out of the gold?
JOSH PATE: I love these questions. I don’t think so. What do you think, Shan?
BURKE: I don’t think so. I think she has hooked up with another rich guy on Outer Banks, and she’s okay. We wanted to be gracious with everybody. Like, they had some contentious relationships but they still grew up with her, she’s part of Sarah’s family, and it’s a happy ending. Everyone’s more or less on good terms. But yeah, I don’t think she got the gold.
“Seductive Charmer”
DEADLINE: Rose seemed like a good, reasonable parental figure until she hooked up with Groff. Who in their right mind would associate themselves with somebody like him?
JOSH PATE: I think old Tony is a seductive charmer.
JONAS PATE: I mean, If you see watch the whole show, you see all the bad sides of him.
JOSH PATE: Shannon and I are, we always described the character of Groff as “tennis handsome.”
DEADLINE: Groff is one of the most irredeemable characters I’ve ever seen on TV. Did you try to humanize him, or he was just there for us to hate him?
JONAS PATE: We like the good villain, right?
JOSH PATE: We toyed with it, and there were elements that we wanted to soften. I think he’s just got a deep psychopathology that’s going on.
There was this book called Blood Will Out that our buddy Walter Kirn wrote. It’s about this sociopathic guy who imitates a Rockefeller, he murders somebody, and Walter, who’d befriended him, goes to see him in prison after he’s been convicted of murder. And he’s like, “Okay, man, you lied to me about everything, and you f*cking killed somebody. And the guy looks right at Walter and goes like, “I didn’t kill him.” He’s still lying.
That’s what we just kept thinking about. Like, wow, this guy can really go all the way.
BURKE: There’s that moment where he has the painting of Larissa, he’s talking to Larissa. I don’t think he’s redeemed, but I think it’s explicable that his original sin is that he married up into Larissa’s family, and then he ends up killing her, and then he’s trying to go back to reverse this thing that he did initially. He’s obviously insane, he’s gone crazy, so not redeemed in any way, but maybe explicable?
The Case Of The Disappearing Kooks
DEADLINE: Can you explain how the Kooks disappeared somehow, and how in the world is Topper now a bartender? Don’t the Kooks have wealth?
BURKE: Well, even wealthy people – they still work as bartenders, they have trouble. The intent was to soften him, to make him more relatable, like he’s actually learned something.
JOSH PATE: I think he’s been excommunicated from his parents a little bit too. He’s had a lot of trouble with his mom and dad, so maybe he got cut off and has to support himself now as a bartender. But again, yeah, to make him a little bit more likable, as Shannon would say.
DEADLINE: But Kooks still live there, they are just not as rich as they were? There seems to be a clear shift in the dynamic on the island.
JOSH: I think the Kooks abandoned the island after the hurricane to a large extent because the island’s destroyed, and what’s happened in the coastal Carolinas is, you can’t get insurance anymore. So they’ll pay you back, but they won’t let you rebuild, and that’s kind of it. Kind of like what’s happening in LA, and so I think, the post-hurricane island returns to more a poorer version of the island.
Acknowledgments
DEADLINE: Any final thoughts about your Outer Banks journey and ending the show on your own terms?
JOSH PATE: We feel really a lot of gratitude to being allowed to end the show in the way we wanted to. A lot of gratitude to Netflix, to Ted [Sarandos] and Bella [Bajaria] and Nne [Ebong], who believed in the show from the beginning, and they largely let us tell the story that we wanted to. So, you’ve been around Hollywood long enough to know that you rarely get to end on your own terms. So, we feel a lot of gratitude for that.

A post by an X user named Sonali (@Sonalimumbai1), who describes herself as a BJP leader and is followed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the platform, went viral last week. The post carries a somewhat blurred black and white image of a group of women dancing atop a table in what seems to be hotel. Sonali implied that one of these women is Congress leader Sonia Gandhi.
The image, posted on August 14, has more than 353,800 views till date. (Archive)
बारबाले चे मूत्र पिणारे असंच बोलणार. pic.twitter.com/C0jpHXHXMa
— 🚩 सोनाली 🚩🇮🇳 (@Sonalimumbai1) August 14, 2026
The post came shortly after Congress leader and Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi on August 14 mocked at the BJP government’s foreign policy and took a jibe at PM Modi’s customary hugs with international leaders.
The remarks triggered immediate backlash from the BJP and its supporters. As a part of that, X user Sonali, posted a video of Indira Gandhi hugging former President of Cuba Fidel Castro. The caption read, (translated from Marathi), “Whenever Rahul talks nonsense, all the misdeeds of his family come out in the open. Now watch this video. In this, Indira Gandhi is hugging Fidel Castro of Cuba. I don’t think anything there is wrong with it. What will the son of a bar dancer say about this? Now what do the sycophants of Congress have to say about this?”
राहुल्या जेव्हा कधी तोंडाने हागतो त्याच्या खानदानाची सगळी कर्म रस्त्यावर येतात.
आता हा व्हिडिओ बघा.
याच्यामध्ये इंदिरा गांधी Cuba च्या Fidel Castro यांच्याशी गळाभेट घेत आहेत.
I don’t think anything wrong with it.
बारबालेचा पुत्र याच्यावर काय बोलणार…??
आता यावर… pic.twitter.com/FVz3c1USL6
— 🚩 सोनाली 🚩🇮🇳 (@Sonalimumbai1) August 14, 2026
After an X user responded to Sonali’s post with derogatory comments, she countered it with the aforementioned image with the caption: “That’s what people who drink bar dancer’s urine would say.”
Fact Check
To verify the authenticity of the image, which was bearing the watermark of Getty Images, we ran a reverse image search on Google. This search led us to the archive of Getty Images, where a clearer version of the same image is available. The caption of this image reads: “Go Go dancing girls help break the beer drought on Rawson Hotel in Auburn on 21 November 1967.”
The image comprises three dancing women. If one zooms in on the image, it becomes clear that none of these women is Sonia Gandhi.
Upon further investigation, we came across a Facebook page named ‘I Grew Up in Mortdale 2223’. On November 17, 2025, the page posted the same image with the caption: “#OnThisDay 17 November 1967, a strike by more than 2000 brewery workers in Sydney led to what was to be known as the “Draught Beer Drought”. When, after 14 days of negotiations, the workers voted to return to work, a group of go-go dancers helped patrons to celebrate at the Rawson Hotel in Auburn. [Photo by Vic Sumner » Fairfax Archives]
This news was also featured on the November 15, 1967, edition of The Canberra Times of Australia.
According to publicly available information, Sonia Gandhi studied at Bell Education Trust, Cambridge, United Kingdom in 1964, where she met and married Rajiv Gandhi in 1968. During her studies, she worked as a part time server at a local restaurant in Cambridge. There is no official record mentioning that she moved to Australia in that time period.
Thus, it can be conclusively stated that an image from 1967 of go-go dancers in Australia was shared by X user Sonali to falsely claim that one of those women was Sonia Gandhi.
Sharing unrelated images to attack the Congress leader is not a new trend. Alt News published a fact-check on March 25, 2019, debunking a similar claim. At the time, BJP supporters circulated an image of actress Ursula Andress from the James Bond film Dr No, falsely claiming that it showed Sonia Gandhi in an “inappropriate” dress.

'I was meant to be there': Off-duty Mountie helps rescue baby, family trapped in house fire
Const. Anton Lorde banged on windows to alert residents, helped man haul out his family as fire raged
Four people — including two teens and a baby — are survivors of a fast-moving house fire thanks to an off-duty RCMP officer who rushed to their aid and helped a desperate man pull his family out of a basement window.
Const. Anton Lorde was on his way home late in the afternoon from his shift on July 18 when he spotted a plume of dark smoke billowing into the sky. It led him to Mount Pleasant Street in the Whitney Pier neighbourhood of Sydney, N.S.
Lorde arrived to find a house being ravaged by fire, with flames shooting out the front, sides and roof. He assumed no one was home because a number of people were milling about. So he immediately started clearing the narrow street for the arrival of fire trucks.
But when he stopped a neighbour to ask about the homeowner, he was told a lot of people lived there, including kids.
"I’ll never forget that — it almost seemed like everything froze,” the 10-year veteran of the RCMP said in a recent interview.
The neighbour pointed Lorde to a backyard where he hopped a fence and began banging on windows of the burning building, going from one to the next in case someone was inside.
Suddenly, hands parted the blinds, and the eyes of a shocked boy looked back at him.
“Probably frightened him with some of the things I was saying for him to get out. Then I lost sight of him because he closed the blinds,” Lorde said.
“At that point, my mind is going a mile a minute.”
He continued to pound on the window, yelling for them to get out and calling for someone to pass him something to smash the glass, when the father of the children appeared.
In an interview at his burned-out property, Peter Magliaro said he was nearly home when he got a call from his niece that his house was on fire.
As he ran between buildings in "unbearable heat," flames burned his cheek, he said.
"You're not thinking, all that was on my mind was the kids."
He started "hollering" to them, knowing they were at home and that his 13-year-old son was likely sleeping because he plays video games at night.
Then Magliaro started kicking in a basement bedroom window before Lorde ripped away the thick blinds to bust out the glass shards.
Magliaro grabbed the four-month-old baby girl from her mother, who is Magliaro's stepdaughter, and passed her to Lorde. He had no idea Lorde — who wasn't in uniform — was a police officer.
Magliaro's brother-in-law, who lives on the same street, helped him haul the rest of the children out the window: his teenaged son, and his stepdaughters, who are 15 and 22.
Some details of the rescue are a blur to Lorde, who hails from Uniacke Square in Halifax. But it was not a solo effort.
“There were a number of us that saved lives. I think the older gentleman bringing it to my attention at the time, and then my natural instincts and training kicked in at that point, and then the father or stepfather coming to assist in a time of urgency,” said Lorde.
Magliaro agreed it was three men pulling together, and praised the Mountie.
"That's big, not too many people would do that with the amount of people that were here that day," said Magliaro. "I mean this guy's right there on my back with me."
Lorde said someone hugged him before he left the scene. Another person shook his hand and called him a hero, but he downplayed the suggestion.
“I was meant to be there,” he said.
The municipality said its fire crews were called at 5:30 p.m. and were on scene within six minutes. Fire crews were able to save the family's cat and a rabbit, Magliaro said.
The fire marshal’s office declined to comment, citing an ongoing investigation, and noted Cape Breton Regional Police are also investigating.
In a Facebook post, Magliaro contends the fire was intentionally set and is offering a reward for information leading to the arrest of “the person or people responsible for setting my house on fire while my children were inside.”
Magliaro said his brother-in-law told him "they heard a bang and then the next thing you know the whole front of the house was engulfed in flames."
With both doors to the home ablaze, "somebody had to have set the fire, and it wasn't from the inside," Magliaro said.
CBC News asked Cape Breton Regional Police about the allegations in Magliaro's Facebook post.
"We cannot speculate on the cause and/or whether the fire was intentionally set; answering those questions is part of the investigation," police spokesperson Desiree Magnus said in an emailed statement.
Magliaro said he's been told it could take six to eight weeks to learn the results of the fire investigation.
Magliaro and his family are now living in a friend's apartment. He said the house was uninsured but he intends to draw from savings to start rebuilding in the spot where he's lived for 35 years.

Madras may be 387 years old, but who doesn’t like to be celebrated on their birthday? Over the years, especially in the age of social media, the days leading up to August 22 have grown increasingly exciting, with residents finding newer ways to tell the city’s story. The outpouring of love is evident in the many heritage walks, talks, exhibitions and concerts that uncover lesser-known facets of Madras, reminding us that it is more than just a place on the map.
Few cities wear their artistic identity as proudly as Madras. From Carnatic music and Bharatanatyam to theatre, literature, cinema and fine art, its cultural landscape has been shaped by generations of visionary creators. As Madras grows another year older, its artistic traditions and cultural institutions offer a window into its spirit.
My own understanding of that spirit began in 1996, the year Madras became Chennai, when I first arrived here. Neighbours and friends in the North warned that the move would be a social climb-down. But I soon discovered that Chennai offered something else: a cultural world that felt, in many ways, richer.
Ever since my school days, I had dreamt of escaping the freezing winters of the North and experiencing the warmth of music during Chennai’s Margazhi, when the city turns unusually breezy and cool. It was also the time when you could spot the finest pattu saris and impeccably draped veshtis. While people across the country geared up to end the year in pomp and style, for Chennaiites, it marked the beginning of a new Season.
What struck me most about Chennai’s kutcheri culture was its lack of pretension. The focus was firmly on the music. Interestingly, conversations at family gatherings and friendly get-togethers revolved not around fashion trends or food, but around who had sung Abheri or Kalyani best or which dancer had drawn a full house.
I soon understood that in this city, art was not merely entertainment; it was a way of life. So, in 2017, when Chennai was included in UNESCO’s Creative Cities Network for its contribution to the performing arts, it only affirmed what residents had long known.
While deeply protective of its artistic traditions, the city has never prevented its artistes from questioning conventions, broadening their horizons and engaging with their art on their own terms. This openness is not a recent phenomenon; it has been part of the city’s artistic temperament for decades.
How else can one explain the founding of an institution such as Kalakshetra by Rukmini Devi Arundale? Established at a time when Bharatanatyam was undergoing a transformation in social perception, Kalakshetra sought to preserve the form’s classical rigour even as it placed it within a new institutional framework.
A few kilometres away, closer to the sea, Chandralekha established her creative hub, Spaces, where she built an experimental practice on the foundations of her Bharatanatyam training. Her bold and radical approach to choreography explored the expressive possibilities of the body and, in the process, redrew the boundaries of the dance form.
Then there was the inimitable Balasaraswati, a powerful representative of the artistic legacy of the heriditary devadasi tradition that had long nurtured and enriched Bharatanatyam.
These pioneering artistes set the stage for succeeding generations of dancers to reimagine the repertoire and discover new possibilities within an ancient dance form.
But the city’s ability to accomodate seemingly opposing artistic impulses was not confined to dance. It has also enabled the kutcheri tradition to thrive, even in the digital era. Few other cities can boast such an extensive network of sabhas, a concert calendar that continues to expand and a steady stream of young entrants willing to take on the challenges of a complex and demanding classical tradition.
Yet, the tradition has not remained unchanged. The duration of a kutcheri has shrunk from four hours to two, and sometimes even less. Mikeless concerts have given way to amplified performances. Artistes are also finding ways to assert their individuality, whether by incorporating modern poetry that engages with social concerns, reinventing presentation style or performing in unconventional spaces. Some, in search of possibilities beyond the conventional concert format, have moved to cross-genre collaborations. What is remarkable is that the city’s rasikas have been accepting of these changes and continue to throng sabhas.
As the art form evolved, instrumentalists, once largely confined to the role of accompanists in kutcheris, gained greater visibility. Exclusive festivals began to showcase their artistry and celebrate their contributions. Ghatam legend Vikku Vinayakram broke new ground nearly five decades ago by joining the iconic East-West band Shakti, inspiring generations of percussionists to explore collaborative music-making and find new avenues for creative exploration.
They have come a long way since then. Two Chennai-based instrumentalists, violinist Ganesh Rajagopalan and kanjira exponent Selva Ganesh, have gone on to win Grammy Awards, taking the sounds and sensibilities of Indian classical music to global audiences.

When someone uploads a photo to the people-search tool ClarityCheck, the website has a clear message: “Your reverse image search is private and secure.” New research, though, shows that the website left more than 9 million image files, including photographs of people’s faces, publicly exposed. And a second misconfiguration publicly exposed people’s email addresses and phone numbers.
Overall, according to findings from independent security researcher Jeremiah Fowler, the exposed ClarityCheck database contained roughly 450 GB of images, including what appeared to be profile images, screenshots, and other photographs of adults, teenagers, and children. All of the images were stored in an unsecured Amazon S3 bucket, with files in folders named “faces” and “profiles,” which could be accessed by anyone online through a URL included in the company’s publicly available website code.
ClarityCheck is one of a number of so-called people-finder tools that have appeared online in recent years. These websites broadly claim to be able to search the web, public records, and other databases to identify individuals. ClarityCheck’s website says it can run searches on phone numbers, email addresses, vehicle identification numbers, and names. Its photo-search page says it can help “identify anyone in a photo” and find social media profiles “in seconds.”
While ClarityCheck secured the giant image database after WIRED contacted the company in July, Fowler warns that it was seemingly exposed for months, and his initial efforts to flag the problem to the company were unsuccessful. Accidental data exposures create risk for any personal information, but particularly for sensitive and unchangeable biometric data like face images.
And while ClarityCheck’s website requires people to attest that they have permission to upload photos to its site, Fowler points out that in practice, people whose faces were exposed may have had no idea that ClarityCheck held their image. After all, he notes, the service is explicitly designed for identification, and people don’t typically seek to identify themselves or people they know.

A post is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) claiming that US President Donald Trump said he had spoken with Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and that the US was in talks to adopt India’s EVM system for the 2028 election. It further claims that Trump praised India’s EVMs as secure and called for an end to mail-in voting. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: Donald Trump said the US is in talks with India to bring its EVM system to America for the 2028 election.
Fact: The viral post is fabricated. In his original post, Trump mentioned CEC Gyanesh Kumar’s interaction with the US administration and praised India’s voter ID system while urging Congress to pass the SAVE America Act. However, he did not say that the US was in talks to bring India’s EVM system to America for the 2028 election. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
To verify the claim, we conducted a Google search using relevant keywords but found no credible reports or official information confirming that US President Donald Trump said the US is in talks with India to bring its EVM system to America for the 2028 election.
We then reviewed the social media accounts (here, here, and here) of US President Donald Trump to check whether he had made the statement mentioned in the viral post. However, we found no post from Trump stating that the US is in talks with India to bring its EVM system to America for the 2028 election.
During this process, we found a Truth Social post (archived) by Trump dated 18 August 2026. In the post, Trump stated that earlier that month, India’s Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar had asked his administration how the US could conduct elections without valid photo ID. Trump also referred to India’s last election, which had 646 million voters, noting that less than 1% voted by mail and that every voter had to provide a valid photo identity document. He concluded by calling for the passage of the SAVE America Act.
The post was also reposted (archived) by US Ambassador to India and Special Envoy to South and Central Asia Sergio Gor on the same day, stating, “President Donald J. Trump is absolutely correct! 646 MILLION voters, every single one, required an ID in India’s last election. Congress should pass THE SAVE AMERICA ACT.” This further confirms that the viral post claiming Trump discussed bringing India’s EVMs to the US is fabricated.
We also found multiple media reports (here, here, and here) about Trump’s post, in which the US President praised India’s election system and called for the passage of the SAVE America Act, referring to the conversation with CEC Gyanesh Kumar. However, none of these reports mentioned that the US is in talks with India to bring its EVM system to America for the 2028 election.
The SAVE America Act (H.R. 7296), or the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act, is a proposed US federal law that would require people registering to vote in federal elections to provide documentary proof of US citizenship and require voters to present an eligible photo ID when voting. The bill was introduced in the US House of Representatives on 30 January 2026 and referred to the House Committee on House Administration. As of 20 August 2026, it has not (here, here) become law. The legislation concerns voter eligibility and identification and has no provisions related to adopting or importing India’s EVM system.
To sum up, this viral post alleging that President Donald Trump said the US plans to bring India’s EVMs for the 2028 election is fabricated.

Kenyan middle-distance runner Faith Kipyegon has brought her season to an early close after failing to fully recover from a hamstring injury. As a result, she will miss next month’s first-ever World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Hungary.
The three-time Olympic champion and four-time world 1,500m champion had been expected to compete at the event, which will feature around 400 of the world’s top athletes in Budapest from September 11 to 13.
“Since the end of May, I have been dealing with a hamstring injury, and unfortunately it needs a bit longer to recover than I had hoped”, she posted on X.
“I will take the time to heal, recover and get stronger,” she added.
The 32-year-old was unable to fully overcome the problem during two important races in July. She placed third in the women’s mile in Eugene, Oregon, earlier that month and said she was competing at 98 percent while hoping to regain full fitness before the season ended.

Shares of Zaggle Prepaid Ocean Services surged 12.15% on the BSE today after veteran investor Vijay Kedia’s broking company Kedia Securities acquired a 1.48% stake in the fintech SaaS company. Kedia Securities bought 20 Lakh shares for around ₹32.94 Cr through a bulk deal yesterday. The shares were purchased at ₹164.72 apiece. Following this, Zaggle shares zoomed nearly 18% to touch an intraday high at ₹195.70 today. The bulk deal came after Zaggle shares faced heavy selling earlier this week following the disclosure of its financial results for the June quarter of the financial year 2026-27 (Q1 FY27) after market hours on August 14 (Friday). The stock slumped 20% on August 17 (Monday). The company also informed the exchanges on August 15 (Saturday) that the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals) had dismissed its appeal against a ₹4.09 Cr income-tax demand for assessment year 2022-23. The I-T department had disallowed certain items, including carry-forward losses, bad debts, and Ind AS adjustments. Zaggle reported a 33% YoY and 57% QoQ decline in its consolidated net profit to ₹17.5 Cr in Q1 FY27. Operating revenue rose 28% YoY but declined 32% sequentially to ₹423.3 Cr. The company said its EBITDA margin declined due to elevated expenses related to its acquisition of enterprise spend management startup Dice Enterprises in May. Zaggle acquired the Pune-based startup’s assets and intellectual property for ₹68 Cr. It said revenue from Dice’s contracts would begin reflecting in its financials from Q2 FY27. The company also incurred employee and other expenses related to the integration of credit card fintech Rio.Money, which it acquired last year and subsequently rebranded as Zagg.Money. Zaggle further attributed the decline in profitability to the transfer of previously capitalised expenses to its profit and loss statement and salary increments for existing employees.

Seven people, including five Americans, were killed when a safari helicopter crashed on Wednesday morning in a remote part of northern Kenya, according to local police and the state department.
Among the dead were an executive with Telemundo, the US-based Spanish-language network owned by NBC Universal, and the director of Ecuador’s national intelligence service.
The helicopter crashed at 9.13am while flying from the Loisaba Conservancy to the Ewaso Nyiro area in Samburu county, according to the Kenya Civil Aviation Authority, which said in a statement that an investigation was under way. It said there were seven people onboard – six passengers and the pilot.
Late on Wednesday, David Nkoroi, the police commander for Samburu, told reporters that all seven people onboard had died.
In Washington, the state department said five of those killed were US citizens. “The US embassy is in touch with local authorities and is providing consular assistance,” it said. “We extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones on their loss.”
The identities of the victims were not revealed but a local television station in Miami, Florida, said that José Suárez, 55, president and GM of several Telemundo stations in Florida, was among those killed.
“We are heartbroken to learn the tragic news that José was killed in a helicopter accident in Kenya,” the NBC affiliate in Miami quoted from a joint statement from NBC Universal and Telemundo leadership.
The helicopter crashed in a rugged area in the foothills of Mount Ololokwe, a popular tourist destination in the country, local media reported. The helicopter, owned by local company Lady Lori Helicopters, was carrying guests with the travel company +Beyond.
Lady Lori Helicopters said in a statement that the aircraft was operating a charter flight when it crashed.
Tropic Air Kenya, a local safari operator, said in a statement that it dispatched two of its helicopters to aid search and rescue operations.
The aviation authority said the aircraft was a Eurocopter EC130 B4.
Ecuador confirmed later on Wednesday that Michele Sensi-Contugi, director of the country’s national intelligence center, died in the helicopter crash in Kenya.
In a statement posted on X, the presidency said: “In this moment of deep sorrow, the government extends its heartfelt condolences to his family, loved ones and close associates.”
Sensi-Contugi was visiting Kenya as a tourist with his wife, Stephany Hollihan Vasconez, who also died in the crash. She was a US and Ecuadorian citizen. They are survived by their two children.
Helicopter crashes have happened with increasing regularity in Kenya, which has a thriving tourism industry that depends on domestic carriers to ferry visitors to distant places like Mount Ololokwe.
In February, a legislator was among six people who died after a helicopter crash in a hilly area of western Kenya.

Shigellosis has surfaced again in Keralam, with a three-year-old child from Kottukal in Thiruvananthapuram district admitted to SAT Hospital with the infection.
Following this, health officials have renewed public health warnings, urging people to be cautious about the food and beverages they consume outside their homes, especially during the festival season.
According to reports, the child had travelled with her family to Nagercoil on August 12. On the way, they reportedly consumed cold drinks from a wayside vendor. The child developed diarrhoea and vomiting the following day and was later admitted to SAT hospital, where she is now recuperating in one of the paediatric wards. The case was confirmed on Tuesday (August 18, 2026).
One more case of shigellosis was also reported from Vizhinjam in Thiruvananthapuram on Tuesday; and three scattered cases from Pazhayannur in Thrissur; Kattipara in Kozhikode and Noolpuzha in Wayanad.
Shigellosis (bacillary dysentery) is a highly contagious bacterial diarrhoeal infection caused by shigella, which is contracted through contaminated food or water. The disease can present with mild symptoms or as severe cases of diarrhoea.
Health officials point out that cases of shigellosis are reported sporadically throughout the year from all districts in Keralam, with some cases triggering small local outbreaks.
The infection spreads through contaminated water, food and contact from infected surfaces.
While shigellosis is self-limiting in healthy adults, it can be fatal for children under five years, in whom the highest mortality is reported. The elderly and immunocompromised individuals are also highly vulnerable.
Symptoms usually appear within one to two days of infection and include fever, diarrhoea, vomiting, nausea, blood in stools, and painful, frequent urges to use the washroom.
The Health department has advised that affected persons use solutions of oral rehydration salts so that dehydration is avoided and that they seek treatment if there is no respite in diarrhoea.
It was in June this year (2026) that Keralam reported major Shigellosis outbreaks, with over 225 cases and six deaths reported from Kozhikode, Malappuram, and Wayanad districts. Outbreaks were officially declared in Kozhikode (77 cases), Wayanad (27), Malappuram (37), Thrissur (15), and Alappuzha (5). Cases were also reported from Thiruvananthapuram (20), Kollam (15), Kannur (14), Palakkad (6), Ernakulam (4), Idukki (3), and Pathanamthitta (1) during June and July.
As of August 18 this year, as many as 441 confirmed cases, 106 probable cases and eight deaths due to Shigellosis have been reported in the State. Last year, a total of 133 cases were reported, with zero deaths.

Three things to know about the $40 trillion federal debt
Sign up for the Planet Money newsletter. The world is confusing. Economics can help.
The Treasury Department reported this week that the U.S. federal debt had reached $40 trillion, an eye-popping level of red ink. Just the annual interest on that accumulated debt now tops a trillion dollars, making it the government's second-biggest expense, behind only Social Security.
Here are three things to know about the deepening financial hole the government is in.
How did the debt get so big?
For years, the government has spent more money than it collects in taxes. Some of that has been driven by political choices — to wage war, cut taxes or provide a more generous social safety net during the pandemic. But much of the growth in spending happens automatically, as baby boomers age into retirement, resulting in higher costs for Social Security and Medicare.
Loading...
Historically, debt as a share of the economy tended to rise during recessions, then stabilize during economic expansions. More recently, the government has run large deficits even when the economy has been growing. The debt has doubled in size since 2017. And now the people who lend money to the government are demanding higher interest rates.
How does this affect me?
The federal debt affects all Americans indirectly, because it limits the government's ability to tackle other priorities. But it also affects some people more directly, by making it more expensive to borrow money.
"When the government borrows this much, and the rates for Treasurys go up, that brings up the rates for everything else, from mortgages to car loans to credit cards," says Michael Peterson, CEO of the Peter G. Peterson Foundation, which advocates for fiscal responsibility. Mortgage rates, for example, tend to rise and fall with the yield on 10-year Treasurys, and the rate on 30-year home loans has climbed near 6.7%, according to Freddie Mac.
Loading...
Is anyone in Washington working to address the debt?
The Treasury Department has taken steps to limit the increase in long-term bond yields. Yields fell on Wednesday after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the department would increase its buy-back program for government bonds.
But the move does nothing to solve the underlying problem, and the effect was short-lived; The yields on 10- and 30-year Treasurys rebounded on Thursday. Earlier, the Treasury had taken steps to prop up the Japanese yen, so Japan would not be tempted to sell some of its own U.S. Treasurys. (Buying bonds pushes yields down, while selling pushes yields up.)
Ultimately, Congress will have to raise taxes, cut spending or — most likely — do both. While some lawmakers used to proudly say they were deficit hawks, fiscal discipline has generally fallen out of favor in Washington. But anxious signals from the bond market could change that.
"$40 trillion should be a wake-up call," said Carolyn Bordeaux, executive director of the Concord Coalition, a deficit watchdog group. "Both parties helped bring us here, and both parties now have a responsibility to change course."

'Ghana was the crime scene': The country leading the demand for slavery reparations
- Published
This year has seen a dramatic change in tone in the global conversation about the transatlantic slave trade.
The demand for formal apologies, debt relief and financial compensation from nations and institutions that benefited from slavery has become increasingly forceful.
In March, a resolution was passed at the United Nations recognising slavery as "the greatest crime against humanity" - though the United States voted against the resolution and every European nation abstained from the vote.
The UK, which alongside Portugal dominated the transatlantic slave trade, has consistently rejected the idea of paying reparations, which is perhaps unsurprising given estimates of what Britain "owes" in damages to nations affected run into many trillions of pounds.
This resistance has not deterred the country that has become the leading voice on reparations: Ghana.
Ghana cannot afford to be silent on ensuring that we hold perpetrators accountable"
It was Ghana that tabled the UN resolution, and in June, a summit on reparations was held in its capital, Accra, with delegates from around 80 countries, who concluded that recompense was long overdue.
"Ghana has always been a pan-African leader. We're the first country to attain independence in sub-Saharan Africa and to prove that it is possible to fight imperial might, and win," Foreign Minister Samuel Okuzeto Ablakwa tells me.
Ghana has been given special responsibility by the African Union to be "champion for reparatory justice" and it is clearly a role the country's political leadership is taking seriously.
In part that is because about 10-15% of the estimated 12 million Africans who were forcibly removed from their homes, torn from their villages, and dehumanised on a scale never before seen, were from what is now Ghana. Even more were shipped from its shores.
"Ghana was the crime scene where these atrocities took place, so Ghana cannot afford to be silent on ensuring that we hold perpetrators accountable," Ablakwa says.
The minister has called for a system of reparatory justice that funds educational grants, venture capital for young African entrepreneurs and research into enduring health issues that some argue may trace their roots back to the severe malnutrition and inhumane conditions of enslavement.
And though he insists that this is not about direct financial gain for African leaders, one of the demands laid out at the recent summit on reparations clearly talked of debt relief and debt cancellation.
He also wants individual institutions that benefited from the slave trade to be held accountable and pay compensation. Among these is the Church of England.
In the 18th Century, the Church's missionary wing ran plantations and owned hundreds of slaves, which helped fund its work across the Americas and beyond.
Many Church of England clergy independently owned slaves, and a recent report by the Church's endowment fund reported the institution made large investments in the slave trade from which it made huge sums of money.
In July, the leader of the Church, the Archbishop of Canterbury Dame Sarah Mullally, visited Ghana in one of her first international visits in the role.
She travelled to Cape Coast Castle, one of the many coastal fortresses that had been run by the British, and where enslaved people were held before enduring the brutal "Middle Passage" to the Americas.
As she toured the dungeons where slaves were held and walked through "the door of no return" through which they were forced before being loaded on to ships, Dame Sarah looked emotional and stopped to pray.
"I felt the weight of the depth of evil that the transatlantic slave trade was. You can't help but be deeply moved by the horrific conditions that people were kept in," the Archbishop said.
She also prayed in a 17th Century chapel that was positioned directly above the dungeons.
"For me that is such a stark illustration of the way the Church was involved in the slave trade," she says. "How can the church have sat above the horrors that were going on below?".
"The Church of England has apologised for the part that we played in the transatlantic slave trade but we've also said there needs to be action that relates to that," Archbishop Sarah said.
The Church has set up a £100m ($135m) social impact fund designed to benefit communities thought to continue to feel the enduring legacy of the slave trade today.
But within the Church, the establishment of the fund has encountered resistance, just as the global push for nations to pay reparations has done.
One of the key counter-arguments centres on the fact that some Africans were themselves complicit in the capture and sale of their fellow people.
But Foreign Minister Ablakwa emphatically rejects this narrative. "I think that there's a strategy to divide and conquer and to create a very contrived confusion," he argues.
He stresses that the entire architecture of chattel enslavement was curated by Western slave-owning powers, who simply utilised local actors to help carry out their plans.
The foreign minister points out that when the laws, insurance policies, and financial architectures of the trade were being drafted, "there was no African at the table".
"We denounce and totally reject those claims that Africans are as guilty and complicit as those who masterminded this whole atrocity," he says.
Yet, within Ghana itself, the conversation around African complicity is far more nuanced, and for some traditional leaders, acknowledging the past is a vital prerequisite part of healing.
King Tackie Teiko Tsuru II, the Ga Mantse, leader of Ghana's Ga people, recently took the step of publicly apologising for his ancestors' involvement in the slave trade.
"I think that the transatlantic slave trade was the greatest crime against humanity, and ancestors also took part as players in that trade," says the king.
The Ga people became middlemen who traded with Europeans. They sold gold, ivory and ultimately enslaved Africans, often those captured in local conflicts, in exchange for the manufactured goods brought mainly by the British and Dutch, including textiles, alcohol and guns.
But the king felt he needed to say sorry not just for his own people's complicity, but the complicity of other Africans too.
"I stand on the same point of apologising on behalf of all traditional authorities and my ancestors and forebears for the part they also played in the slavery of our brothers and sisters.
"It has affected lives and societies up to now, and to be able to go forward, you have to look at your past. It dawns on us to admit our fault and correct it," he says.
The king believes strongly in the need for those who benefited from the slave trade to pay reparations and acknowledges that he, too, needs to commit to making financial amends.
"I believe that it underpins a state of moral courage and credibility."
For the Ga Mantse, admitting fault does not dilute the guilt of European empires; rather, it solidifies Africa's moral standing and sets an example as to how to move forward.
But Ghana is leading the way in another aspect of trying to heal the damage done by the slave trade. The country has run a high-profile campaign inviting the African diaspora - particularly African-Americans - to visit the continent.
It has been promoted as a means of bringing people together in the shared story of their traumatic past, with "reparations" quite literally focussing on "repair" at a very human level.
Yaw Asare, now a Ghanaian PhD student at Howard University, previously worked within the President of Ghana's Diaspora Office, which ran the campaign.
Initially, the gathering of black people from across the globe was, he felt, "a beautiful, profound experience devoid of capitalist motives". But he says in some respects the initiative soon morphed.
"The Ghana Tourism Authority also latched on to it and then used it to enhance their tourism project," Asare explains, saying the initiative started to become less about "repair" and more about hitting tourism quotas.
Asare says the campaign has often viewed the returning diaspora simply as a means of foreign cash flow, raising prices and negatively altering local economies.
"Now (local) people are finding that they cannot afford basic things," Asare says, describing how local Ghanaians were economically sidelined.
More devastatingly, he feels the commercialisation of the initiative overshadowed the deep, psychological work that is desperately needed for locals as well as "returning" members of the diaspora.
"We are dealing with humans, we are dealing with people. We cannot reduce them to, 'come see this site, pay this entrance fee'," Asare says.
He also questions - in an initiative that was partly supposed to be about addressing the trauma of Africans in the diaspora - why they were required to pay entrance fees at the same rates as European tourists at, for example, the coastal castles where slaves were trafficked.
He says all of this means a missed opportunity to address deep-rooted trauma some of which he feels is etched into the very geography and psychology of modern Ghana.
"Go to Jamestown (in Accra), people are huddled together because there is the fear of 'if I live far away, I could be taken'," Asare says, pointing to how centuries-old concerns dictated why people built their houses so closely together.
Jamestown is one of the oldest districts in the city, a community originally built around a British coastal fort where slaves were brought, traded and then sent on ships to the Americas.
For Asare, true reparatory justice must prioritise human connection and healing over financial transactions.
"We have to remove the band-aid and then look at the sore, the gaping wound that's present," Asare says about what he sees as real "reparations". "And see how we can dress it and nurse it and heal".

A demand has been made to install advanced screening systems in government and private blood banks in Kerala in the wake of reports about the spread of HIV, Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C infections among college students in some parts of the country.
Organisations working for the welfare of patients suffering from blood disorders in the State point out that blood banks across India have relied heavily on voluntary blood donations from college students, considering them one of the safest donor groups for many years. Thousands of patients suffering from thalassemia, sickle cell disease, haemophilia, aplastic anaemia, leukaemia, and other blood disorders depend on regular blood transfusions for their survival. However, reports about the increasing prevalence of viral infections among young donors has turned out to be a cause for concern, says Kareem Karassery, president of the Blood Patients Protection Council, Kerala.
The Collegiate Education Department and Visvesvaraya Technological University in Karnataka recently took steps to conduct integrated health camp for HIV testing and counselling for students in all engineering and degree colleges based on a request from the Karnataka State AIDS Prevention Society (KSAPS). This followed reports about the rapid spread of HIV infection among youth in the 18-35 age group there. According to the KSAPS, the number of infected people in this age group rose from 44,500 in 2023-24 to 66,600 by 2025-26. According to a report, more than 7,000 young people in the 18-25 group in Karnataka have been diagnosed with HIV. Reports of blood transfusion-related infections were recently reported from Haryana and Madhya Pradesh too.
Sources say that there are thalassemia-infected children in Kerala as well who were diagnosed with Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C after blood transfusion. However, they are reluctant to reveal their names. One of the HIV-infected children recently underwent a bone marrow transplant surgery in Bengaluru. Doctors say that the child will take another two years or so to test negative for HIV.
Mr. Karassery says that although the donated blood undergoes mandatory screening, many blood banks in the country still do not have access to advanced nucleic acid testing technology, which can detect infections during the window period — the time between a person getting infected with a virus and when lab tests can find it.
Letter to Nadda
In a letter to J.P. Nadda, Union Minister for Health and Family Welfare, Mr. Karassery said that patients who require lifelong blood transfusions are a vulnerable group. He urged the Centre to launch a nationwide awareness campaign on the prevention of HIV, Hepatitis B, and Hepatitis C, with special focus on adolescents and college students. Details about blood-borne infections, their modes of transmission, and preventive steps should be introduced in the higher secondary school curriculum. NAT screening facilities should be set up in government and private blood banks across the country. Also, a national policy should be developed to provide adequate financial compensation, lifelong medical care, and rehabilitation support to patients who contract infections through blood transfusions.

A Stubbornly Naive Group of GOP Senators
A small caucus of non-MAGA Republicans keeps falling for the president’s flimsy promises.
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
For many observers of American politics, the past few years have been disillusioning, knocking down hopeful beliefs about what the people of the United States will support or tolerate. Even some of Donald Trump’s backers have become disaffected.
Yet somehow, a small caucus of non-MAGA Republican senators has managed to remain preciously naive about the president and the administration he runs. No matter how many times Trump or his aides show who they are and how they operate, these senators seem flabbergasted and saddened.
No case illustrates the ease with which they are fooled like the confirmation of Todd Blanche as attorney general. Blanche was confirmed last week on a 50–49 vote, but only after GOP Senators Thom Tillis and John Cornyn extracted a written assurance from Blanche that a $1.8 billion fund for payouts to Trump allies would not proceed. Senator Bill Cassidy also wavered, but said he was persuaded by the vow. (All three men will leave the Senate at the end of this term: Tillis is retiring, and Cornyn and Cassidy lost primaries to Trump-backed challengers.)
This weekend, Blanche was interviewed on Meet the Press. Kristen Welker asked whether he could “pledge that the Justice Department will always act independently of the White House.” Blanche refused—likely an honest answer, given his demonstrated willingness to follow Trump’s lead, but one that should worry anyone who believes in the rule of law; witness Trump’s repeated demands for political prosecutions, irrespective of evidence. Yet Blanche insisted to Welker that Trump “will never ask me to do something unethical or illegal. He never has. He never will.”
That might reassure someone whose political memory stretches back only as far as early August. But anyone old enough to remember the slush fund, or Blanche’s starring role in negotiating it (as laid out by Federal Judge Kathleen Williams in May), would know that Trump not only has asked Blanche to do something unethical, but that Blanche complied. In order to vote to confirm, Cornyn, Tillis, and Cassidy had to convince themselves first that Blanche’s conduct in that case is not indicative of his basic moral compass; and second that he would be more accountable once permanently confirmed by the Senate than he was when he still had to win over their votes. If Trump finds or attempts to find some way to resuscitate the slush fund—as some experts believe he might—many people will be dismayed, but only this trio of guileless senators will be shocked.
Cassidy’s willingness to vote for a Trump yes-man is all the more puzzling because he voted to convict Trump in his 2021 impeachment trial, and because the president led the charge to defeat him in a primary. (The impeachment vote was Trump’s main reason for targeting him.) But Cassidy has a long record of credulity. As my colleague Nicholas Florko has reported, Cassidy—a physician—cast a deciding vote to confirm Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr., but only after the nominee made promises about preserving the existing vaccination regime, a pledge he promptly broke. On ABC’s The Week this past Sunday, Cassidy said “it’s pretty evident” that Kennedy’s vow was a lie. And on CNN’s State of the Union, he called the White House’s latest vaccine move, attempting to unbundle the measles, mumps, and rubella injection, “a crazy, stupid thing.” Senator John Barrasso of Wyoming, another doctor, voted for Kennedy and has since been upset about the administration’s anti-vaccine steps. Who could have foreseen that the prominent vaccine skeptic would undermine federal vaccination policy?
Two other moderate Republicans, Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski, voted against Blanche’s confirmation, issuing statements that noted the politicization of the Justice Department under his watch as acting attorney general. But they are not always so clear-eyed. Murkowski delivered one of 2025’s most unintentionally hilarious statements when she cast a crucial vote to pass Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act through the Senate. “My sincere hope is that this is not the final product,” Murkowski said in a statement. “This bill needs more work across chambers and is not ready for the President’s desk. We need to work together to get this right.” Naturally, that didn’t happen; the mystery is why she thought the White House, or Mike Johnson’s House, would improve the bill once she’d surrendered her leverage.
Collins, however, is the dean of the credulous caucus. The Mainer, who faces a tough reelection campaign this fall, is perpetually concerned about Trump-administration actions, but seldom ready to actually use her power. Collins is a rare pro-abortion-rights Republican who previously said she wouldn’t support any Supreme Court nominee who opposed Roe v. Wade. In 2018, she voted to confirm Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who said Roe was “settled as precedent.” When Kavanaugh was part of the majority that voted to overturn Roe in 2022, Collins lamented the ruling but now says she didn’t regret her vote for Kavanaugh and would do it again. More recently, Collins helped pass a huge appropriation for ICE with few strings attached, then expressed dismay at the use of the funds to buy “shock gloves” for agents. Even her vote against Blanche was symbolic, because he had enough votes to be confirmed without her.
One could easily write these senators off as cynical, but if they’re acting for political gain, it’s not working well: Cassidy’s and Cornyn’s mild deviations from Trump led to the end of their careers; Tillis’s retirement helped him avoid what might have been a stiff primary challenge. Many of their concerns appear earnest. Perhaps they really just are that gullible, unable to adapt to a Trump age that is leaving them behind. In defending his Blanche vote, Cassidy shrugged off attacks: “I’ll be criticized for this vote. What’s new?” But voters might reasonably expect that their elected officials are savvier about the world than a babe in the woods.

Good morning. After the news about Moderna and Merck’s mRNA cancer vaccine came out yesterday, someone resurfaced a great Sharon Begley story on personalized cancer vaccines from early 2016. I recommend reading it if you’re interested in a primer on “turning your cancer against itself.”
Major cancer group cancels alcohol fundraiser
The American Cancer Society has canceled its upcoming Wine and Spirits Industry’s Gala, a spokesperson confirmed to STAT’s Isabella Cueto. The news came less than two months after Isa and our colleague Lev Facher reported that the group had for years raked in at least $22 million from wine and liquor executives, creating at times an unsettling conflict of interest given alcohol’s known links to cancer.
“Can you imagine the American Cancer Society hosting a tobacco industry gala? This is basically the same thing,” said public health professor Michael Siegel, who called the decision to cancel the gala a wise one. Read more from Isa.
Who is Heidi Overton?
While health secretary Robert F. Kenendy Jr. has been the public face of the MAHA movement and the Trump administration’s health care efforts, Heidi Overton has been the top policymaker behind the scenes, STAT’s Chelsea Cirruzzo and Daniel Payne report. Now, President Trump has nominated Overton to run the nation’s food and drug agency.
Overton has spent years as a Trump loyalist, having served in the first administration. Some industry leaders are worried about her close association with former director Marty Makary and the White House. On the other side, many MAHA activists are convinced Overton is to blame for stalled and slow-moving policy initiatives. So how might Overton fare at the FDA? Read more.
When hospital chatbots actually come in handy
Modern electronic health records are bloated. As health systems started experimenting with generative AI tools, the idea was that the technology could be used to find a needle in a haystack — the key piece of information, hidden in pages of records, that could explain a clinical mystery and potentially save a patient’s life. Today, a number of health systems are moving toward broad implementation of chatbots for EHRs. But as STAT’s Katie Palmer reports, it turns out that solving diagnostic mysteries is the least of their selling points.
The dominant application of AI chart summarization tools is decidedly less cinematic: Doctors are using them to save time as they prepare to see patients. Still, questions remain about how many errors are worth accepting in the name of efficiency, and ideally, the rare needle-in-a-haystack discovery. Read more from Katie on where things stand.
Inside a 5-year-old brain organoid
For years, scientists at Harvard rented space to the longest-living brain organoids on record. But they rarely actually studied them, as the longevity became an intimidation. “What if you make a mistake and the experiment doesn’t work and all of a sudden you cannot go back to a sample that is so unique?” Paola Arlotta, a developmental biologist in the lab, told STAT’s Megan Molteni.
Eventually, one junior scientist had the courage to analyze the specimens. A study published yesterday in Nature details what the team found. Over more than five years, the organoids had developed and matured in the same way that our own human brains do. Read more from Megan on the science and how it could be used.
Contrasting legal decisions on gender-affirming care
Last week, a federal appeals court ruled in favor of the Justice Department’s efforts to obtain gender-affirming care patient records from the telehealth company QueerDoc. While most judges have categorized such requests as overreaching or for an improper purpose, two out of three judges on the panel ruled that there was nothing out of line about the QueerDoc request. (Some legal experts believe that the case could be a candidate for en banc review, meaning the entire court would review the case again.)
The QueerDoc case was the first of many quashed requests to be appealed by federal law enforcement. But since oral arguments were made in March, the DOJ has taken a different approach to other subpoenas, concentrating its efforts in a Texas district court with a strong conservative reputation. At least one subsequent criminal subpoena, for records from NYU, has been temporarily blocked by a New York federal court.
Most recently, transgender patients and advocates logged a victory in court, as a district court struck down a Trump administration rule that attempted to exclude gender-affirming care from the “essential health benefits” that Affordable Care Act marketplace plans are required to cover. While only a handful of states explicitly include transgender health care in their list of essential benefits, the care is often covered as part of another protected category, like prescription drugs. The judges ruled that the administration did not use proper procedure to propose the change — an argument that probably won’t work against a similar rule barring Medicaid from covering the services.
